segments.text: Spain built high-speed AVE rail to replace short-haul flights between its biggest cities, only
to watch the connecting traffic that sustained dozens of smaller regional airports disappear.
This is unintended consequences, episode 115.
Spanish planners and successive governments turned to high-speed rail because the country's
geography and growing economy made the existing mix of roads and conventional rail feel increasingly
inadequate for moving people between major centers.
The goal was to create fast, reliable links that would reduce reliance on domestic aviation
for the busiest corridors while lowering overall tribal times and emissions.
At the time, Madrid, Barcelona and Madrid-Sovil were among Europe's busiest short-haul air
routes, and shifting those passengers onto trains appeared to be a straightforward substitution
that would free airport capacity for longer international flights.
Decision-makers worked with traffic forecasts that treated the two modes as direct competitors,
rather than parts of an interconnected network.
The investment also aligned with broader European Union priorities that favored rail for distances
under roughly 500 kilometers.
Planners could point to the arithmetic of passenger volumes on those two dense corridors, and
see clear room for a faster surface alternative that would also cut fuel burn per trip.
They could also see that conventional rail and road links already existed, but were too
slow to capture the time-sensitive business traveler.
The Madrid-Sovil AVE began service in 1992, and the Madrid-Barsalona line followed in
2008 after years of construction that included new tunnels and viaducts, engineered for 300 kilometers
per hour operation.
Early ridership on the new services exceeded many projections, and airlines quickly removed
aircraft from those city pairs.
Proponents pointed to the train's punctuality and city center to city center times, as clear
evidence that the policy was working.
Passing your counts on the Seville corridor rose steadily once the trains offered three
hour journeys that competed directly with the one-hour flight plus airport procedures.
Airlines responded by cutting frequencies and then withdrawing aircraft types that had been
dedicated to the route, freeing them for other markets or retirement.
Once the airlines withdrew from the Madrid-Barsalona and Madrid-Sovil air routes, the network
affects spread outward.
Regional airports that had depended on passengers changing planes in Madrid or Barcelona for
onward connections lost that traffic almost overnight.
Without enough remaining demand, carriers reduced or eliminated service to those smaller fields,
and several facilities recorded sustained drops in movements that eventually led to closure.
Cities without an AVE station found themselves farther from the national transport spine than before,
because the air connections that had previously compensated for their location were no longer viable.
The infrastructure had not simply substituted one mode for another,
it had reconfigured the entire topology of air service by removing the economic
justification for thin routes that depended on hub feed.
Consider the arithmetic at a typical regional airport.
If 40% of its departures had been feeder flights whose passengers connected onward from Madrid,
the sudden disappearance of those connecting passengers could drop total movements below the
level needed to cover fixed costs for ground handling, security staffing, and runway maintenance.
Airlines facing their own yield calculations then pruned the remaining direct flights because
load factors fell. The result was not a gradual decline but a step change loss that made continued
operation uneconomic for both the airport operator and the carrier.
Once the pattern of airport clutters and lost connectivity became visible in traffic data,
regional governments and transport authorities began examining ways to restore links through
subsidized routes or improved bus and conventional rail feeders.
Some airports received public service obligation support to maintain minimal service,
yet these measures could not fully recreate the previous network density.
Public service obligation contracts have kept a handful of routes alive,
but they require ongoing budget allocations that were not part of the original AVE business case.
When a new infrastructure mode captures the highest volume routes,
it can remove the economic foundation that supports thinner connecting services across an entire network.
Treating one mode as a simple replacement for another overlooks how carriers and passengers
actually combine modes to reach secondary destinations. Planners who model only the direct
corridor risk underestimating the system-wide topology changes that follow.
